candidate.blueprint_topic: Advance directives, self-determination, and integration of goals into the plan of care
candidate.educational_objective: Explain that advance care planning should begin proactively in cirrhosis, can continue alongside liver-transplant evaluation and disease-directed treatment, and should document the client's values, goals, surrogate decision-maker, and future treatment preferences before decision-making capacity is lost.

options.A: No. Advance care planning is an ongoing process for discussing and documenting values, goals, a surrogate decision-maker, and future treatment preferences; it can occur alongside transplant evaluation and disease-directed care.
options.B: Yes. Advance care planning is appropriate only after transplant-directed treatment has been stopped and the client has chosen hospice care.
options.C: Advance care planning should wait until hepatic encephalopathy causes loss of decision-making capacity so the family can make decisions then.
options.D: Only specialty palliative-care clinicians should discuss advance care planning; hepatology and transplant-team clinicians should avoid these conversations.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. AASLD defines advance care planning as a proactive, ongoing, collaborative process of medical decision-making that includes identifying surrogate decision-makers, discussing illness and prognosis, eliciting values and treatment preferences, and documenting goals through advance directives. AASLD specifically states that disease-directed care, including liver-transplant evaluation and listing, does not preclude palliative care and that hepatology clinicians should provide basic advance care planning. Current AASLD guidance also recommends starting advance care planning early in cirrhosis and preferably before hepatic decompensation or loss of decision-making capacity. B is incorrect because advance care planning and palliative care can coexist with transplant-directed or other disease-directed treatment; hospice is a distinct, comfort-focused model. C is incorrect because waiting until decision-making capacity is lost defeats a central purpose of advance planning. D is incorrect because AASLD encourages hepatology clinicians and other members of the care team to participate in primary palliative care and advance care planning rather than reserving these discussions exclusively for specialists.
candidate.source_claim_supported: AASLD directly supports proactive, iterative advance care planning in cirrhosis; early documentation of values, goals and surrogate decision-makers; participation by hepatology clinicians; and continued ACP/palliative care during liver-transplant evaluation or other disease-directed treatment.
